description_full: Analog Devices, Inc. engages in the design, manufacture, testing, and marketing of integrated circuits (ICs), software, and subsystems products in the United States, rest of North and South America, Europe, Japan, China, and rest of Asia. It provides data converter products, which translate real-world analog signals into digital data, as well as translates digital data into analog signals; power management and reference products for power conversion, driver monitoring, sequencing, and energy management applications in the automotive, communications, industrial, and consumer markets; and power ICs that include performance, integration, and software design simulation tools for accurate power supply designs. The company also offers amplifiers to condition analog signals; and radio frequency and microwave ICs to support cellular infrastructure; and micro-electro-mechanical systems technology solutions, including accelerometers used to sense acceleration, gyroscopes for sense rotation, inertial measurement units to sense multiple degrees of freedom, and broadband switches for radio and instrument systems, as well as isolators. In addition, it provides digital signal processing and system products for numeric calculations. The company serves clients in the industrial, automotive, consumer, instrumentation, aerospace, defense and healthcare, and communications markets through a direct sales force, third-party distributors, and independent sales representatives, as well as online. The company was incorporated in 1965 and is headquartered in Wilmington, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Analog Devices, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $192.8B market cap on $11.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 64% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $4.3B in free cash flow — roughly 39 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.12× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.2×.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 27% operating margin runs 20pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.14x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 77% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 1.29, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.07 vs 5y 1.35), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.3B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 24% in the 2022 bear market and 55% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $222 (margin of safety -80%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $154 to $327 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 47.3 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 29.6 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 45.1 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 107% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 32 covering analysts target $472 on average, 19% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.57).
It runs a 64% gross margin and converts 39% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 2.12x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 16.0% of revenue on R&D and 2.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($3.7B of cash against $8.6B of debt), with interest covered 9.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 9.0, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 143 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
Goodwill makes up 56% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.8% over 3 years, 14.5% over 5 years and 12.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
At current returns, reinvesting 61% of profits supports about 4.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 18.3% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 4.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 50, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.3% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 93%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (76 sales, net $17.4M sold).
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 16.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 24,500 employees, each generates about $450K of revenue, 1.2x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 11.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $175K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.5M (12x revenue per employee).
